translation:
Jivanji Maharaj, who had come to Gujarat from Malwa with his company of saints, arrived at a village called Vadsar (a village in Padra taluka). From there he set out and went to a village called Samiyala, where he held hari-kirtan (hymn-singing to Hari) and an ochhav (festival celebration). During his stay here, Gopaldas of Dhaniyav came, bringing with him a man named Haribhai. (This Haribhai was Jivanji Maharaj's personal scribe, the one who wrote down every single word of the Guru in the form of a text, and the original compiler of this Samagam.) In this way the members of the devotee circle kept increasing. On the way, Gopaldas of Dhaniyav recited to Haribhai a sakhi (couplet) of Kabirji:

_Kabir nadiya jal koila bhai, samudra lagi aag; machhi jake taruvar chadhi, uth Kabira jaag ||1||_ (Kabir says: the river's water has turned to charcoal, the ocean has caught fire; the fish has climbed a tree — rise, O Kabir, wake up!)

Haribhai (of Aritha, from Dhaniyav), who was eager to have the Guru's darshan (sight of the holy one) and receive his teaching, recited this sakhi of Kabir while on his way to the Samiyala ochhav, expressing his own inner anguish: to have the Guru's darshan and receive his teaching, the river of maya's hopes and cravings within him had now burned down to charcoal, and a fire had broken out in the ocean of this world; and his restless, fish-like mind, to escape this raging fire, had now climbed up onto the great tree of the true Guru (Sadguru), who alone can carry one across the ocean of existence. So now — O Kabir, that is, O soul — wake up, become alert, and accept the shelter of the Sadguru.

This Haribhai, tormented by the pain of separation from the Guru, would express his inner anguish through Kabir's sakhis as he walked along the road. When Jivanji Maharaj, engaged in satsang (holy company), saw him and observed these signs, he too expressed — through a sakhi of Kabir — the anguish he himself felt in separation from a devotee like Haribhai who belonged so closely to him.

_Kabir mo virahinika piv mua, daag na diya jaay; maansahi gali gali bhui para, karank rahi lapataay ||2||_ (Kabir says: like a grief-stricken woman whose husband has died, whose flesh has melted away and fallen to the ground though she was never burned by fire, so that only her skeleton remains clinging together — such is my state.)

Seeing a devotee close to him like Haribhai, Jivanji Maharaj says through this sakhi of Kabir: just as a grieving woman whose husband has died — even if her body has not been burned by fire — has the flesh of her worldly attachment to happiness, as it were, melted and dropped away to the ground, so that hardly any flesh at all is left clinging to her bones, leaving her in a death-like state, so has separation from a devotee like you brought me to that same condition.

In this way the Sadguru, so full of feeling for a worthy disciple, expressed his affection, and then accepted Haribhai by giving him the mala (rosary) and tilak (forehead mark of initiation). Under the heading "Bhekh" (the ascetic's garb and vow), Jivanji Maharaj spoke this sakhi:

_Maans gali gali bhuya pade, tvacha haad tan jaay; man gale bin Jivana, Raghupati nahi adhaay ||32||_ (Even if the flesh melts and falls to the ground, and the skin, bones and body too are ruined, says Jivan, Raghupati is not satisfied unless the mind has melted [in devotion].)

Even if a person takes up the ascetic's garb and causes the body such suffering that the flesh melts away and falls to the ground, and the skin, bones and body too are ruined — however much such suffering is endured — God is not pleased unless the mind has melted in loving bhakti (devotion).

There is a sakhi of Kabir:

_Kabir guru dajha chela jala, kathan birahaki aagi; tinuka bapura ubara, gal pure ki laagi._ (Kabir says: the Guru burns, the disciple burns, in the harsh fire of separation; only a poor small remnant is left unburned before the fire reaches all the way up to the throat.)

For a disciple suffering in the ocean of this world, the Guru whose heart holds deep affection is himself burning; such a Guru has become anguished by separation from the disciple. And the poor disciple, in separation from the Guru, is burning in the threefold fire of maya. This is the fire of separation between Guru and disciple — only a small, wretched portion of it remains unburned before it reaches all the way up to the throat. Only a little hope is left that the suffering of this separation between Guru and disciple will end. Kabir says:

_Kabir paani manhi machhali, chadhi parbat dhaay; agan piye pushta bhai, jal piye mar jaav._ (Kabir says: the fish that lived in water ran and climbed the mountain; by drinking the fire it grew strong, but by drinking that water it would have died.)

In the ocean of this world, the fish that is the restless mind has left the water of sensual craving and run up onto the mountain of loving devotion. On this mountain there was a fire of separation, kindled for the attainment of God through love — and by drinking of that fire the fish was revived and refreshed. But had it remained drinking the water of sensual craving, it would have fallen into the cycle of birth and death.

Having given Haribhai the mala and tilak at Vadsar, Jivanji Maharaj then came to Shahpura. Jivanji Maharaj loved staying at this Shahpura very much, because a great saint like Mota (elder) Gopaldas lived there. Praising Shahpura highly, Jivanji Maharaj says:

_Gaam hamaro Shahpuro, jahan sakal sant sukhdhaam; Sadguru hamare Jivana, sol kalasu Shaam._ (Our village is Shahpura, an abode of happiness for all the saints; our Sadguru, says Jivan, is Shyam [Krishna] endowed with sixteen kalas.)

Nana (younger) Gopaldas says: our village is Shahpura, an abode of happiness where Jivanji Maharaj, Sant Gopaldas, and Jivanji Maharaj's other disciples all find in abundance the joys of loving bhakti and satsang. Our Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, who is Krishna endowed with all sixteen kalas (attributes/powers), resides here in Shahpura.

_Sadguru sadesa mokala, kachabacha sab aav; naam chintamani Jivana, je bhave so paav._ (The Sadguru sent word: let all the little ones and grown-ups come; the Name, says Jivan, is the wish-granting gem — take from it whatever pleases you.)

Nana Gopaldas says: Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj sent us this command — all of you, young and old, little ones and grown-ups alike, come to my satsang; the Name, filled with loving devotion, is the wish-fulfilling gem (chintamani) that grants all your heart's desires, so through it, obtain whatever loving devotion is dear to you.

_Baal budhaku Jivana, Ram bhajanki aash; shoorveer bhaagi chale, daante pakadi ghaas._ (From child to elder, says Jivan, all held the hope of Ram-bhajan; the valiant ones broke away, taking straw between their teeth [surrendering the old ways].)

Under the heading "Shura" (the valiant one), Jivanji Maharaj says: those devotees, from children to elders, who showed great courage, stood against ritualism and the path of the Vedas, and — holding to the hope of devotion to Ram — accepted my welcome, are blessed. As for the rest, who used to display valor in trying to attain liberation through the strength of ritual, the Vedic path, scriptures and Puranas, along with their relatives — taking the straw-like, worthless thing that is ritualism and the Vedic path between their teeth, that is, surrendering, admitting defeat — they were beaten before loving devotion and fled, abandoning the valiant path of loving bhakti.

_Shahpare sant seviye, nirakar naam adhar; bhagat het Jivana, Raghupati lino avatar ||78||_ (At Shahpura we serve the saints, our support the Name of the Formless One; out of love for his devotees, says Jivan, Raghupati has taken this incarnation.)

Das Ang (the Devotee's Section)

Nana Gopaldas says: in the hope of devotion to Ram, we shall keep the company of saints like Sant Gopaldas and Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj here in Shahpura — saints who have no form or shape, the Name alone being their one support, existing only in the form of the Name; and it is that same Ram who, for devotees like us, has taken incarnation in the form of Jivanji Maharaj.

For disciples such as these, where the Guru feels such affection for his own people and the disciple in turn pines away for the Guru, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, even in the height of summer, kept a field of val papdi (a variety of bean) green, so as to feed them with this food as prasad. In this way Haribhai and Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj also carried on farming so as to arrange excellent food for everyone. Blessed is such a Sadguru, and blessed are the disciples who receive the grace of such a Sadguru; we too have been blessed by receiving the grace of Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj.

Swami Ranchhodlal Odhavlal of Hansapura has written in his notebook, page 157:

[Kavit Kundali:]

_Shahpur game jai juo, Dhadhar sarita teer; aamraghata vriksha kunjame, sant base sudhir ||1||_
_Sant base sudhir, sant bodhaj aape; sharanagat sahu Jivana, trividh taap ja kaap ||2||_
_Harshit Haridas kahe, sant charan man mudit bhayo; Dhadhar sarita teer, Shahpur game jai juo ||3||_
(Go and see the village of Shahpura, on the bank of the river Dhadhar; there, amid a grove of mango trees, dwells a steadfast saint who himself gives true teaching, and removes the threefold suffering of all who take his refuge, says Jivan. Delighted, Haridas says his mind has been filled with joy at the coming of the saint's feet — go, on the bank of the river Dhadhar, to the village of Shahpura, and see for yourself.)

Go to the village of Shahpura and see — it lies on the bank of the river Dhadhar. There, in a grove of mango trees, dwells a saint of profound steadfastness, who gives the true teaching of loving bhakti. He removes the threefold affliction of the souls who take refuge in him. Full of joy and delight, a devotee of God, Haridas, says that his mind has been filled with happiness at the coming of such a saint's feet — so one should go to the village of Shahpura on the bank of the river Dhadhar and have the same experience as he has had.

That is to say, Kabirji states that those who are separated from Parbrahm (the Supreme Being) must go to some place or other — that is, to a Guru — in order to attain him. And when such seekers mistake some ordinary guru or wandering yogi for a true saint, they truly become entangled: afterward they can neither embrace him nor let him go. Once wound around him in affection, one is later forced to repent — a matter Kabirji has illustrated with a fine and fitting example. Thus, had seeking devotees such as Gopaldas, Santdas, Haribhai and others wandered off elsewhere, they might never have been able to meet Jivanji Maharaj at all, or would have had to wander a great deal. And even if they had eventually met him, it would have cost them much sacrifice and time. This is exactly why one should understand and reflect carefully on the words of capable great souls like Kabirji or Jivanji Maharaj before taking any further step. If one acts without thinking and becomes entangled, one can neither speak of it nor weep over it — one ends up in a state of belonging neither here nor there. As we have already seen, one Naranadas Khatri, who came with Jivanji Maharaj, sat waiting patiently for thirty-two years like Shabari, yet never became entangled anywhere. In the same way, the other devotees who came were also, in this same manner, searching for a capable person (a Guru) like Jivanji Maharaj. Jivanji Maharaj has truly said —

_Guru kije vichaarke, jehi batave Raam; Sarayu teere Jivana, je nagar Ayodhya gaam ||1||_
_Hari bhaje hari na paiye, sab aap aapkun ghaay; guru samsa bin Jivana, kaal jhapete jaay ||2||_
(One should choose a Guru only after much thought — one who can show the way to Ram, says Jivan, on the bank of the Sarayu, in that city and village called Ayodhya. Even by chanting the name of Hari one does not attain Hari, if all are only harming themselves; without a true equal to a Guru, says Jivan, one falls prey to Death.)

That is to say, a Guru too must be chosen only after much careful examination and thought, not by being taken in by pomp, show, or outward splendor.

Thus, having spoken this sakhi of Kabirji, Jivanji Maharaj gave the kanthi (neck-thread) and tilak to Haribhai, who had come with Nana Gopaldas, in the village of Vadsar. From there Jivanji Maharaj proceeded to the village of Shahpura, together with his company of saints — those who had left home and household to walk out with their Guru.

After arriving at Shahpura, Gopaldas, overwhelmed with feeling, says that this village of Shahpura is now truly their homeland, since it is here that they find the happiness of saintly company; that is, one should live wherever there is a Guru and the company of saints. What comparison is there between Chanderiya in Rajasthan and Shahpura? What a spirit of renunciation this is! Gopaldas, who had left behind his homeland and his ancestral property to walk out with his Guru, embraces Shahpura like an unshaken warrior, and from there proclaims that Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has now arrived, and that he has carried the message: whichever brothers, sisters and children wish to come, let them come; such an occasion will not come again. This was not a blind race after a Guru, nor blind imitation — it was a celebration filled with eager longing for the attainment of the true path. Here, on every side, an occasion of joy has spread; it is the joy of having gained something far greater than what was lost. It is in praise of this very joy that Jivanji Maharaj says —

All those who left their native homeland and came, at Jivanji Maharaj's invitation, together with their children and families, into the presence of the Guru — all of them have now come relying solely upon, and trusting in, one Guru. Therefore he is their father as well. And Jivanji Maharaj used this very word throughout his life — that all these little ones and elders, these "child-cowherds" (bal-gopal), have gathered here in order to attain "Ram", the Supreme Being. Moreover, all who have come here are truly valiant; those who proceeded by the strength of ritual observances and vows have been defeated.

In this way Jivanji Maharaj praised the spirit of renunciation of the company of saints who had walked out together with him. They are not cowards but valiant ones; they are like tiger cubs, never ones to feed on grass. Thus saints of true feeling, filled with a genuine longing to know dharma, gathered here at Shahpura. This was a small gathering, a little religious council. Here, today, the dharma of Namdev and Kabir was about to come into existence in a new form and color. All who had gathered to lay its foundation were valiant ones. At the head sat Jivanji Maharaj, and in his presence a new tradition was being built.

After Sadguru Shri Jivanji Maharaj had finished his travels across India, he made his permanent dwelling at Shahpura and spread there a firm and steadfast dharma, by which those trapped in the slavery of the confused ritualism, brahmanism, and so on then prevailing in the world could practice devotion to Vishnu in a very simple and guileless way. He rescued from ruin those who, in the name of a self-serving religious convention, would take to tempting yet treacherous paths like the path of ritual works or the path of yoga in the practice of true bhakti. He disproved the belief that liberation must be attained through jnana (knowledge), and determined what true knowledge really means.

_Sarasvati shodhi Shahpare, jaiso Dhadharko neer; Sadguru vachane Jivana, koi ek paave teer ||156||_ (Sarasvati has been purified at Shahpura, like the water of the Dhadhar; through the Sadguru's word, says Jivan, some rare one alone reaches the far shore.)

[Guru]

Sarasvati, that is worldly learning, teaches both truth and falsehood — one may receive teaching in virtue as well as in vice. But just as we filter and purify the water of the Dhadhar before using it, so Jivanji Maharaj purified Sarasvati (learning) of its impurities and made it clean at Shahpura; that is to say, the Sadguru separated true bhakti from the vice-ridden maya surrounding it and discovered pure devotion to Vishnu alone, and only those rare ones who follow the Sadguru's teaching will manage to cross over and reach safely to the far shore of the ocean of worldly existence.

_Je sajaniya sukh podhate, so jan gaye Kedar; guru shabda bin Jivana, mile na dooji vaar ||157||_ (Those companions who once slept in comfort — those very people, says Jivan, went to Kedar [the Himalayas, to their death]; without the Guru's word, one does not get a second chance.)

Even people like the Pandavas, who enjoyed the happiness of being God's own kinsmen, ultimately went to melt away their bones in the Himalayas, because they had not received the Guru's teaching. Even though they were as fortunate as to be Krishna's own kin, Krishna did not come to them a second time in the Himalayas to give them knowledge like that of the Gita, in order to save them from rebirth in heaven and so on. Such a fate does not befall one who has a Sadguru like Jivanji.

In this way Jivanji Maharaj shattered the many false delusions such as melting one's bones in the Himalayas or dying at Kashi, and kindled true bhakti at Shahpura. Jivanji Maharaj says —

_Kabir kede pragate, jagma Jivandas; dhaja bandhi dharma dridhaviyo, jam kinkar pame traas ||1||_ (Doha 19)
(After Kabir, Jivandas appeared in the world; he raised the flag and made dharma firm, so that even the servants of Death grew afraid.)

After Sadguru Kabirji, Jivandas (Jivanji Maharaj) appeared in the world, and by "raising the flag" — that is, by making a firm and resolute proclamation — he strengthened the true dharma, so that even the servants of Yama (death) grew afraid, since now there was no longer any possibility of a dharma-corrupted sinner falling into their grasp.

"To raise the flag" means to spread one's fame, to make known publicly what was hidden. Jivanji Maharaj issued a proclamation of Kabir's tradition — he threw down a challenge, and made a firm resolve.

Jivanji Maharaj says that he has come into this world after Kabirji, and walks forward along the path Kabirji showed. The only difference is this: the boundaries that Kabirji had not been able to establish — because of which Kabir's line of thought gradually grew weak after his lifetime and began to split into many branches — Jivanji Maharaj, in order to preserve it in one definite form, binds it under a single banner and fixes its boundaries. Because of this, the servants of Yama and corrupt elements are struck with fear.

"To raise the flag" means to establish boundaries, to make definite policies and rules, to prepare a constitutional structure, and to make loving bhakti firm. Jivanji Maharaj, together with his inner circle of devotees at Shahpura, drew up the constitution of the "Uda Dharma Ramkabir Parampara" (the Ramkabir tradition of Uda-dharma). His devotees had a very large part and cooperation in this. Moreover, it is not the case that all the policies and rules were made all at once; wherever and whenever a difficulty arose and a need presented itself, he began to frame policies and rules to meet it. This process went on for a number of years, and only afterward could this tradition come fully into being.

_Kanto haath Kabirke, sakal dharma toliyo; jap tap tirath daan, ta mule mitho choliyo ||18||_ [Doha]
(The scale is in Kabir's hand, weighing the whole of dharma; against japa, tapa, pilgrimage and charity, at its root it is found the sweetest of all.)

The dharma that Jivanji spread on a firm footing was compared with other observances such as japa (recitation), tapa (austerity), pilgrimage and so on, and Kabir was set up to weigh it impartially and give judgment upon it; and Kabirji, declaring the true result, said that this dharma of Namdev-Kabir, spread by Jivanji Maharaj, is the best of all, better than japa, tapa, pilgrimage, charity, vows, and the rest.

Nana Parekh has written this doha to fill the gap left where the account of the time of Jivanji Maharaj's departure to his heavenly abode was lost in a Samagam manuscript that had been burnt, and in commenting on it he has written that —

This dharma is the original, eternal one (sanatan). Other dharmas are flimsy husk. I have looked at the three worlds and the twenty-one universes, but nothing else can measure up to this dharma. By "other dharmas" is meant japa, tapa, pilgrimage, charity, and so on.

Carried away by fervor while praising his own dharma, he used disparaging words for other dharmas, calling them flimsy husk. Excess of self-praise is considered improper. Compared to dharmas of japa, tapa and so on, our dharma is better in every way — in other dharmas many difficult conditions come about, whereas we have fared well by comparison; that is the intended meaning. For this reason, Pujya Yadunath has removed the words about "flimsy husk" from the second edition of Pancharatnamala. One's own dharma alone is considered the best dharma; another's dharma, however good it may appear, need only be considered as simply not suited to us — that much is enough to say.

In discussing this dharma of our Namdev-Kabir, which cannot be matched by anything in the three worlds, Jivanji Maharaj, showing what is superior in our dharma compared to other dharmas, says that just as Vaishnav Jivandasji has made us Vaishnavas, so too the merchant (Vanik) community also calls itself Vaishnava. But he discusses at length what difference there is between our Vaishnavism and the Vaishnavism of others.

Among Vaishnavas, three kinds are recognized. But the Vaishnav dharma that Jivanji Maharaj established, according to the dharma of Namdev-Kabir, is different (distinct) from other Vaishnavism. Not only that — it is the very reverse, the opposite, of all the others; and so it is written in the parcheri (hagiographic account) of Jivanji Maharaj:

_Sabte ulti raah chalai, aad antki katha sunai._ (He set a path going that is the reverse of everyone else's, and told the story of the beginning and the end.)

(Panchratnamala, p. 239)

Vaishnavas speak of exclusive, one-pointed devotion, but they cannot give up the path of the Vedas and the path of ritual works. Hence they cannot give up the worship of the many devas either, and so exclusive devotion never truly comes about. For this reason, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj was the very first to oppose the Vedic path and ritualism, to reject the Brahmins' authority, and to call for giving up japa, tapa, vows, charity, and idol-worship altogether. Thus Sadguru Jivanji started a path exactly opposite to that of all worldly people, and he explained his original form as an incarnation of Krishna and how he had now manifested as Jivanji.

We have already discussed the four sampradayas (traditions) earlier, but according to another view, the four sampradayas are considered to be: 1) the Vishnu sampradaya, from Vishnuswami; 2) the Ramanuj sampradaya, from Ramanuj; 3) the Madhva sampradaya, from Madhvacharya; and 4) the Vallabh sampradaya, from Vallabhacharya. In all of these, the principal path is the worship of Vishnu, whose other name is the Bhagavat doctrine. We too hold to devotion to Vishnu alone, but we are entirely distinct from these four kinds of Vishnu-devotees, because all these sampradayas practice devotion to Vishnu through the threefold-guna (three-quality) form of bhakti, whereas we believe in practicing devotion according to the fourth guna, which is beyond the three gunas.

_Kabir trividh lok trigun bhaje, Brahma Vishnu Mahesh; jaisa guru jaakun mile, taisa de updesh._ (Kabir says: the people of the three worlds worship the three gunas — Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesh; whatever kind of Guru one finds, he gives teaching of that kind.)

People who practise the threefold devotion worship the deities of the three gunas — Brahma, Vishnu and Mahesh. Whichever Guru, holding to whatever quality, a person happens to find, that Guru gives him teaching to practice devotion accordingly.

But even if someone is a Vaishnava practicing devotion to Vishnu, one should not simply mix with him thinking that he too is a Vaishnava like oneself, because —

_Bhagati boho bhaantki, jinke bohotek bhed; bin viveke malvo tahaan, man paave ati khed._ (Devotion is of many kinds, among which there are many differences; to mix into it there without discernment brings the mind great sorrow.)

Hit Harivansh says that devotion to God is also of many kinds, and there are many differences within it; therefore, if one mixes into it without truly understanding it, one becomes unhappy.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj has explained how many kinds of Vaishnavas there are. Among the three kinds of Vaishnavas, the Bhagavat dharma is predominant. Hence, apart from the three-guna kinds of devotion — rajasi (passionate), tamasi (dark/ignorant), and satvik (pure) — they are unable to know a fourth kind of devotion. Kabirji says in a pada (hymn) in raga Sorath —

_Tera jan ekadh koi, kaam krodh mad lobh vivarjit, Haripad chine soi; Rajas tamas satvik kahiye, e tino teri maaya; chotha gunkun je nar chine, so nirbhe pad paaya ||1||_ (Your true devotee is one in a rare few — one who is free from lust, anger, pride and greed, and who alone recognizes the state of Hari; rajas, tamas and satva, these three, are but your maya; but the man who recognizes the fourth guna attains the fearless state.)

Your true devotee will be only some rare one, who is free from lust, anger, pride and greed, and who can understand your bhakti; because the three gunas — rajas, tamas and satva — belong to your maya, but the man who can understand the fourth guna that exists beyond them can attain the fearless state, that is, your own abode.

Here at Shahpura, as this company of saints gathered together in this way, a religious tradition was established that could be matched by nothing in the three worlds. This is truly the dharma of Namdev and Kabirji. Who can understand it? We shall now discuss that question. Vaishnava devotees are of three kinds: 1) Pravah-margi (the path of the flow), 2) Pushti-margi (the path of grace), and 3) Maryada-margi (the path of law/discipline). These three kinds of Vaishnavas have been described by the commentators on the Shrimad Bhagavat. Hence, devotion to Vishnu can be practiced in three ways — rajasik, tamasik, and satvik — but no one knows the fourth kind of devotion to Vishnu; so, giving a sakhi, he says —

_Rajas tamas satvik, e teen gunme sansaar; chothe gunko Jivana, so Sadguruko parivaar ||1||_ (Rajas, tamas, satvik — the whole world lies within these three gunas; whoever belongs to the fourth guna, says Jivan, is the family of the Sadguru.)

That is, Jivanji Maharaj says that the universe runs by means of three gunas — sattva, rajas, tamas — that is to say, all of creation in this world remains subject to these three gunas. But those who are devotees of Hari, the true nij-jan (own people) of Parbrahm, are beyond the three gunas; Jivanji Maharaj calls these the ones belonging to the fourth guna, that is, those who, having transcended the three gunas, have gone for shelter to the Sadguru.

That is, as we have already seen in the third chapter, only he who worships Parbrahm having gone beyond the three gunas attains him (Bhagavad Gita, chapter 14, verses 18, 19, 20). The state of this matter is set forth and explained here — that the nij-jan, that is, those who have gone for shelter to the Sadguru and who are subject to none but Parbrahm alone, such devotees of Parbrahm go beyond all three gunas, and even while living in the world they remain set apart from everything.

_Kabir teen svabhavi boho mile, chotha mile jo koy; sabai pyare Ramke, baithe parvas hoy ||2||_ (Kabir says: many are found of the three-natured kind, but if any of the fourth kind can be found, all such are dear to Ram, sitting ever subject to him.)

Kabirji says that many people practicing devotion to Vishnu with a nature of the three gunas can be found, but the fourth guna, which is beyond the three gunas — if one can find any such practitioners of exclusive devotion, they are devotees who are exceedingly dear to God, and they live by going for shelter to Hari, Guru and saints, conducting themselves according to their command.

_Jo dekha so teenme, chotha mile ne koi; chotheko pargat kare, harijan kahiye soi._ (Whatever I saw, it was in the three; the fourth is found in none. Whoever manifests the fourth, he alone is called a harijan.)

Wherever one looked in the world, everyone was found engaged only in the threefold-guna kind of devotion; no one was found practicing devotion in the fourth guna, transcending the three gunas. But whichever devotee holds to the fourth guna, he is called a harijan (a person of Hari).

Jivanji Maharaj traveled everywhere and observed that at every place there were Vaishnavas practicing only the three-guna kind of devotion to Vishnu. He presents here whatever observations he made about them. Among the three kinds of Vaishnavas he saw were: 1) those of the Pravah path, 2) those of the Pushti path, and 3) those of the Maryada path — thus, according to the three gunas, three kinds of Vaishnavas were found. None of these three kinds of Vaishnavas are able to know the fourth kind of devotion to Vishnu. Therefore he compared the dharma of these three kinds of Vaishnavas with attention to how devotion to Vishnu was practiced across all four ages (yugas). He examined how God was viewed by people's understanding in the four ages, and how liberation was understood in each of the four ages, and how the various philosophical schools (darshan shastras) explained the understanding of God in each of the four ages — discussing all such details, he attempted to arrive at a comparative judgment.

Kabirji too had already established this same point earlier. Jivanji Maharaj explains that much has already been said and written about the three gunas, and indeed the whole world lies confused, absorbed in them; but one cannot find anyone belonging to the fourth guna who has gone for shelter to the Sadguru, and if by chance one does find such a person, it is a matter of very great joy — very few people indeed have gone for shelter to a true Sadguru — because all such people are truly nij-jan of Ram. Moreover, their nij-jan, whom no worldly element can touch, are free from everything; they are fearless — and if one finds such nij-jan, one can peacefully sing the praises of Hari.

In keeping with this spirit, Jivanji Maharaj gathered the true jan (people/devotees) of Hari at the village of Shahpura, in order to preserve a lofty tradition of dharma. Here too he weighed and established a dharma with which nothing else could be compared. A natural question arises here: why did Jivanji Maharaj establish a new dharma? As we have already seen earlier, in chapter nine, going up onto the high peaks of the Himalayas, Jivanji Maharaj, having seen during his travels across India how people's lives were being scorched by various afflictions, made a resolve — and that resolve he fulfilled here today. One part of it was this: he demonstrated how Kabirji's words could be put into practice in the world in a more practical and true-to-life form, on an experimental footing. He began to show, by living it in his own personal life, how the practical form of Kabirji's thought was to be followed.

Today, the sampraday which we know by the name "Ramkabir Uda Bhakt Parampara" was not composed complete in a single day or within some fixed span of time — its period of formation was very long. Its beginning took place on Vikram Samvat 1688, Aso Sud 15 (Sharad Purnima), and its full flowering, that is, its complete development, would extend until Samvat 1734, Shravan Vad 8! Its formative period continued right up to Jivanji Maharaj's last breath, as we shall see further on in the commentary on the Samagam. Here, with the company of saints with whom Jivanji Maharaj arrived at Shahpura, the emergence of a new tradition had begun in his presence — it was a new experiment, the beginning of a new process.

In this way, at Shahpura he weighed and established such a dharma of devotion to Vishnu that no dharma like it could exist in all three worlds. For this, Jivanji Maharaj first of all studied the dharma of the four ages — Satya Yuga, Treta Yuga, Dvapar, and Kali Yuga. The text's compiler, Haridas of Nadiad, notes that he examined the dharma of the four ages, described the Supreme Lord of each of the four ages, described the four kinds of liberation, and described separately the philosophy of each of the four ages.

That is, whatever Jivanji Maharaj had gained and experienced in his life up to this day, and whatever he had studied of the scriptures during the four years of rest he spent in the presence of Guru Gopaldasji, and besides that, whatever he had seen from the sannyasi he had earlier accepted as his guru — all of this he now had to distill into its essence here. What was the essential distillation of all the scriptures — the Vedas, the Aranyakas, the Upanishads, the Puranas and so on? Was it "the art of living life"? If the answer to all this was "no", then none of it was of any use at all. In life something was lacking, and moreover the mass of humanity had been bound in such fetters that they had been made helpless and cowardly; into such a mass of people, a new spark of consciousness had to be given once again. For this, it was extremely necessary first of all to know the limits of all the scriptures — which Jivanji Maharaj now proceeds to describe.

_Kaljug aayo Jivana, nirgun bhakti prakaash; Satyug Treta Dvaparma, karma dharmaki aash ||1||_
_Satyug Treta Dvaparma, nij bhaktke paas; ab kaljugme Jivana, main bhole bhaktko daas ||2||_
_Satjugma Hari shvet the, Trehetama Hari peet; Dvaparma Hari shaam varan, Kalijug roop viparit ||3||_
_Satyug Treta Jivana, Vaikunth hamaro vaas; Dvaparma Gokul vasu, kaljug jahan nij daas ||4||_
(Das — 39-40-41-42)
(Kali Yuga has come, says Jivan, and with it the manifestation of nirgun [formless] bhakti; in Satya, Treta and Dvapar there was the hope of ritual karma and dharma. In Satya, Treta and Dvapar he was near his own devotee; now in Kali Yuga, says Jivan, I am the servant of the simple, guileless devotee. In Satya Yuga Hari was white; in Treta Hari was yellow; in Dvapar Hari was dark in colour; in Kali Yuga his form is the reverse. In Satya and Treta, says Jivan, our abode was Vaikunth; in Dvapar he dwelt in Gokul; in Kali Yuga, wherever his own devotee is, there he dwells.)

First of all, the dharma of the four ages, the Supreme Lord of the four ages, the liberation of the four ages, and the philosophy of the four ages have been shown here through the sakhis above. In ancient times, Vedic ritual practice held very great importance; yajnas and similar rites were organized by sages, kings, and the local populace, and very large numbers of people would gather. Disagreements over Vedic yajnas and Vedic mantras did occur even in those days, but their extent was quite small. First of all comes a sage named Kautsa, who used to say: "yadi mantrarthapratyayaya, anarthakam bhavati iti Kautsah; anarthaka hi mantrah" (1-5) — the Nirukta-author Yaska had to bear the opposition of the sage named Kautsa. Kautsa says that if one is to derive meaningful sense (validity) from the mantras — of the Vedic Rigveda and so on — then they are meaningless, because the mantras themselves are without meaning (that is, no fruit is obtained by reciting the mantras).

In this connection Kautsa carries on a lengthy discussion. We need not consider it in full — let us look at just one example.

_"Svadhite ma enam hinsih" ityaha hinsan._ (Nirukta 1-5) ("O axe, do not harm him!" — so he says even while harming him.)

"O axe, do not strike it!" — such words are themselves violence: that is, at the time of a yajna, when an innocent animal is about to be offered up on the sacrificial altar, this mantra is spoken, and then the axe is brought down upon the animal's neck. On the one hand it is said, "O axe, do not strike it (the animal)," while on the other hand it is killed right there. Ritualist Brahmin scholars give a dry explanation of this, saying, "Violence occurring within a yajna is not to be called violence" — but this is like the saying about one who speaks like a madman and one who listens like a madman. Many Brahmins say that reciting the mantra while wielding the axe causes the animal no pain. This is not a defense we can accept. We need not discuss this further, but the violence and sinfulness that entered in the name of yajnas and such rites were entirely without purpose; moreover this was sinfulness carried out in the name of religion, and it was of no use whatsoever. For this reason Jivanji Maharaj did not accept the Vedic ritual of yajna. Furthermore, in those yajnas where no violence occurred, vast quantities of grain were offered into the fire. On the one hand, the ordinary people of the world would be writhing for lack of food to eat, while on the other hand there was this waste. Therefore that religion is useless in which violence occurs, or in which precious grain and the like are misused. Furthermore, over all these scriptures, only the so-called Brahmins alone had authority, and however sinful a Brahmin might be, he was still considered pure! Is this something acceptable to reason? Further on, we have also not accepted the doctrine of various deities, nor has Jivanji Maharaj accepted the various theories of liberation — which we shall examine further ahead. So we do not discuss it at length here.

Finally, there are the various scriptures also known as the darshan-shastras (philosophical treatises). But there is no single agreed view among these scriptures — lacking unanimous consent, these scriptures generate mutual contradictions.

_Bhakti charachar upji, ane swami karoni pasaay; akhil vishramat ek huiye, dhaiye garuo raay ||1||_ (Devotion arose throughout all that moves and does not move, by the grace of the Master. Let the whole come to rest as one; let us hasten to the great King.)

That is to say, when the Patan Vaadi (garden/enclosure) was laid out, the plots (kyara) of these various differing sects were made outside the garden. They were not given entry inside the garden.

Thus none of all this was of any use for the exclusive Vaishnavas, so Jivanji Maharaj determined that they should not be accepted. Giving an example for this, he states that in Satya Yuga the four Sanaka-adi (sages beginning with Sanaka) held sway — namely, 1) Sanaka, 2) Sanandan, 3) Sanatan, and 4) Sanatkumar — these four are called the mind-born sons of Brahma. According to the ancient Puranic story, at the beginning of creation Brahma produced these mind-born sons. All four of these kumaras (youths) were men of knowledge. Therefore, so as not to be deluded by the maya that Brahma had fashioned, they kept themselves bound to a five-year-old boy's span of life throughout their existence. These four brothers never separated; they always wandered together. Once, while wandering, they went to Vaikunth. By the power of their yogic ability they passed through six gates of Vaikunth, but at the seventh gate the gatekeepers named Jaya and Vijaya, who stood guard there, stopped these four sage-youths from entering. At this the sage-youths, blinded by pride in their knowledge, cursed the gatekeepers.

The story is a very long one; we need not concern ourselves with it. Jivanji Maharaj has called the Sanatkumaras "thieving merchants," which we shall see further on. For now, the episode that has come up here — the mind-born and body-born sons of Brahma, including Sanatkumar and the rest — is mentioned by Jivanji Maharaj in order to explain the nature of devotion to Vishnu and why devotion to Vishnu is the very best and ought to be followed. Before going further, let us recall the earlier point: knowledge blinds one with pride. Because the Sanatkumaras were men of knowledge, they became blinded by pride. In failing to observe the discipline that one should not enter another's home without asking permission, they went astray in the pride of their knowledge, and thereby incurred fault. In this way, cursing anyone or invoking a mantra against someone also wastes one's own power. For this reason, the path of knowledge or the path of tantra is of no use; only bhakti is free of pride. But remember — the bhakti of the learned is the lowest of all, and as for hostile devotion (vairi bhakti) within it, that should not even be spoken of. Jaya and Vijaya, made miserable by the curse of Sanaka and the others, and wishing to attain liberation swiftly, asked for vairi bhakti, that is, devotion practiced in the spirit of enmity toward Parbrahm, in which they came — first as Hiranyaksha and Hiranyakashipu, second as Ravana and Kumbhakarna, and third as Shishupala and Dantavaktra — as Jaya and Vijaya; and having sinned again each time, they departed once more.

Brahma, the creator, wished to bring forth and expand the world through the Sanaka-adi sages. But all four of them became lifelong celibate brahmacharis who never wasted the least particle of their seed, and so his wish was not fulfilled. Therefore Brahma produced Marichi, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Bhrigu, Vasishtha, Daksha, Angiras and Narada. The Bhagavat describes the expansion of creation in this way; and these sons were produced from Brahma's body (kaya), whereas the ones produced from his mind had failed to fulfill Brahma's wish. So he also produced other sons and daughters from his body.

Jivanji Maharaj is not much concerned with all this; rather, his purpose has to do with the process of human life after the creation of the world. Among these, some are urdhvareta (those who retain and conserve their seed), while others are dravya (those who procreate through bodily seed) — in this way the world's expansion continues. Those who remain lifelong celibates, or who live without the act of procreation, appoint a successor after themselves, whereas those who live according to the world's rule of procreative duty extend their lineage by producing sons and so forth. That is to say, everyone leaves behind a legacy when they depart. In all this there are so many divisions and branches that deciding which direction to take is not merely difficult but an extremely arduous and hard task. One must think it through with intelligence and choose the true path — otherwise one is liable to go astray somewhere. It is for this very reason that Jivanji Maharaj, quoting a Puranic verse, says —

_Pura Satyayume vevi Vishunmatavadinah, Chagatti Vishnumevevam gnatva Sarveshraram svayam ||40||_ (O Devi, in ancient times, in Satya Yuga, the followers of the pure doctrine, knowing Vishnu alone to be the Lord of all, worshipped him.) [Note: the printed Sanskrit of this line is damaged/unclear in the source; the transliteration above follows the printed text as closely as possible.]

O Devi (Parvati), in the earlier Satya Yuga, the followers of the pure doctrine, knowing Vishnu alone to be the Lord of all, worshipped and revered him alone.

In comparing the dharma of the four ages, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj discusses the dharma of Satya Yuga through commentary on this shloka. In Satya Yuga, truth predominated. Sanaka and the others — that is, the mind-born sons of Brahma — along with his body-born sons, were of two kinds: one kind were urdhvareta, that is, unbroken celibates, and the other were of sexual generation; sixty thousand sons of this latter kind have been reckoned as the sons of Pitruloka (the ancestral realm). All of these have been identified as followers of the dharma then prevailing in Satya Yuga.

That is to say, Shiva, addressing Parvati, says: O Devi, in the earlier ancient times, when it was Satya Yuga, all human beings, considering Vishnu alone to be the Supreme Lord, Parbrahm, worshipped and revered him. Moreover, no one ever acted falsely, nor practiced unrighteousness; everyone conducted themselves according to their own dharma. If anyone did act unrighteously, he was punished — his head was cut off. Because of such severe punishment, people were afraid to commit offenses, and the rule of truth prevailed; people conducted themselves truthfully. This was the age of Sanaka and the others. After this age come Treta and Dvapar in turn.
